title: I'm a psychologist who studies couples: People in the happiest relationships do 1 thing differently after time apart—whether it's hours, days or weeks
description: There's a two-minute window every evening when couples can either strengthen their bond with each other or unknowingly weaken it. In my experience as
body: There's a two-minute window every evening when couples can either strengthen their bond with each other or unknowingly weaken it. In my experience as a psychologist who studies couples, what separates the happy couples from the unhappy ones isn't necessarily how often they argue or how much time they have together. It's whether the two people are genuinely in contact with each other's lives.Partners in happy relationships know what the other one is really going through, week after week. The unhappy ones have often slipped into a kind of parallel coexistence, where they share a home and a calendar and not much else.That difference can be built or lost in moments that may feel too small to matter. I call them "reentry moments." What 'reentry moments' look like"Reentry moments" are the first minute or two when a couple comes back together after time apart. These reunions follow any period of temporary physical separation, whether that's a workday, a weekend away with friends or a four-day work trip. They serve three key functions: Coaxing your partner out of their head and into the present momentGauging where your partner is emotionallyGetting an update on your partner's day (or weekend or week)Let's say your wife mentioned in the morning that she had a presentation that day. You get home and see her, as usual, with her laptop on the couch. You ask her, "How was your presentation?" She stops typing, sets the laptop on the coffee table and tells you that no one really responded to it, and just thanked her and moved on. She spent the rest of her afternoon turning the presentation over in her head, trying to figure out what went wrong. Connecting as soon as you reunite keeps you from misreading each other. If your wife is still thinking about the presentation and you ask whether she booked the rental car for your trip next week, the annoyance in her response can sound like annoyance with you. You might snap back, and now you're arguing about the rental car when neither of you cares about it.There's a longer-term benefit, too. When your partner knows the first few minutes at home will be met with interest rather than judgment or indifference, they don't have to decide what's worth telling you and what to keep to themselves. They can just walk in knowing they're entering their safe landing space.Why skipping a 'reentry moment' mattersEarly in a relationship, nobody has to work hard to harness this moment. You simply want the details of your partner's day, and if you get the three-word version, you ask again. Years in, you may stop following up.You might slip into a routine where you share a greeting, ask a question about dinner or tomorrow's schedule and go about your evening. Nothing overtly unkind happens in that exchange, and both partners might describe it as "fine." But you know slightly less about your partner with each flubbed reentry. After a few hundred repetitions, you start working from an out-of-date picture of your partner. You don't know their new manager has suddenly started checking in on them three times a day. Or that they got into it with their sister on the phone an hour ago. So when they're unusually quiet at dinner, you might assume that something is wrong between the two of you. Skipping this small but crucial moment makes it harder to understand and anticipate your partner's needs, whether that means taking over a chore, canceling a plan or leaving them alone for an hour. Being well-meaning but uninformed might look the same to your partner as not caring. Eventually, you can lose more than just information; you start losing the close connection you share with your partner. How to reconnect with your partner after time apartGetting it right means deliberately stepping out of the "How was your day?" routine and trying something different:Be specific. "How was your day?" asks your partner to sum up eight hours on the spot, a daunting task, which is why it usually gets a one-word answer. Ask about something you already knew was happening that day. "Did your manager say anything?" shows you remembered what was on their mind yesterday. It's also much easier to answer honestly, and can lead to a more meaningful exchange. Follow up. Once they've told you something, keep going with it rather than moving to another subject. In my experience, a single follow-up question tends to get you further than several new ones. Tell your partner if you're depleted. If you have nothing left to give right at that crucial moment, say so rather than going quiet, because "I want to hear about it, I just need 20 minutes" lands very differently than silence.Make sure it runs both ways. Couples tend to fall into roles here without realizing it, where one person does most of the telling and the other does most of the listening. Usually, that's just a matter of who has more energy in the evening. But it means the listener's own day gradually stops getting shared.Act on it. All of this only counts if something comes of it. If you learn your partner had a difficult week and then carry on exactly as you were, the conversation hasn't done much for either of you. What makes a good "reentry moment" worth the effort is that it gives you something to act on, whether that's letting them sleep in the next day or planning a special date. Over time, taking these steps can be part of what keeps two people attuned and responsive to each other rather than simply living side by side.Mark Travers, Ph.D., is a psychologist who specializes in relationships. He holds degrees from Cornell University and the University of Colorado Boulder. He is the lead psychologist at Awake Therapy, a telehealth company that provides online psychotherapy, counseling and coaching. He is also the curator of the popular mental health and wellness website Therapytips.org.

title: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy has stroke and is in the hospital, office says
description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., conducts a rally outside the U.S. Capitol to demand the Senate take action on gun safety on Thursday, May 26, 2022, in the
body: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., conducts a rally outside the U.S. Capitol to demand the Senate take action on gun safety on Thursday, May 26, 2022, in the wake of the Robb Elementary School shooting in Texas. Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., appears at left.Tom Williams | CQ-Roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesSen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was hospitalized Saturday after suffering a stroke at his son's hockey game, his office announced on Sunday.Murphy is "awake and alert," according to a statement from his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt."Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game. He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment," Herwitt said.Johns Hopkins Hospital's main campus is in Baltimore, though it has other locations in and around Washington."The doctors are encouraged by his progress," Herwitt said. "We are optimistic he will make a full recovery."Murphy, who came to the Senate in 2013, is not up for reelection on Tuesday, but he's been crisscrossing the country campaigning for Democratic candidates, with recent stops in Michigan, Minnesota and Florida. He was due in New Hampshire on Sunday to campaign with Democratic Senate candidate Rep. Chris Pappas.He's seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate and is a prolific Democratic fundraiser.Murphy, 53, spent six years in the House before running for the Senate. He rose to national prominence as an advocate for stricter gun control laws in the wake of the Sandy Hook shooting, which occurred in his home state. He's been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump and has opposed the war in Iran and the White House's deportation policies.He's one of multiple sitting senators to suffer a stroke in recent years. Democratic Sens. Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland each had a stroke in 2022. And Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., who was then running for office, suffered a stroke just days before his state's Senate Democratic primary."Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy. I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a fellow Connecticut Democrat, posted to X on Sunday.This story is developing. Please refresh for updates.

schema.headline: Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy has stroke and is in the hospital, office says

title: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries
description: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without interventi
body: Maryvit Luna - CNBC | Getty imagesSocial Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years.Without intervention before then, the Social Security retirement trust fund, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which helps pay benefits to eligible workers and qualifying family members, will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, the program's trustees said in a June report.At that time, the trustees project retirement benefits will be cut by 22%.The Congressional Budget Office has a more dire forecast, anticipating the retirement trust fund may run out sooner, in mid-2032, and that retirees may see larger benefit cuts, at 26%, upon insolvency. Beneficiaries may see an average $500 cut to their monthly benefits across the U.S. based on a 24% benefit cut, according to a June report from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. In 29 states, retirees would see even bigger average reductions, according to the nonpartisan organization focused on educating the public on fiscal policy issues. Senators elected this November will be in office in 2032, when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits. Their ability to right the ship is crucial for retirees and the economy. But it's not a sure thing given the political climate inside the beltway."The attention on 2032 is appropriate in the sense that that is when beneficiaries and future beneficiaries will see and feel the consequences of inaction," said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a public policy think tank focused on promoting bipartisan cooperation."Nothing gets Congress to move like that type of deadline," he said.Of course, brinksmanship and political deadlock may stymie efforts. Congress could opt to kick the can down the road, rather than enact changes to shore up Social Security — which may require tax increases, benefit cuts or a combination of both.If lawmakers decide to combine Social Security's retirement and disability trust funds, the depletion date may move to the third quarter of 2034, when benefits may be cut by 17%, according to Social Security's trustees.Akabas said any delay by lawmakers would have consequences: Social Security's shortfall would continue to increase. There could also be consequences for the economy, he said.In 2023, Social Security benefits generated $2.6 trillion in total economic output and supported more than 12 million jobs, according to 2025 research by the National Institute on Retirement Security, a Washington, D.C., based non-profit, non-partisan organization.A 19% benefit cut could reduce gross domestic product by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to the NIRS research.Moreover, failing to muster Social Security reform would prompt bond market strain, according to research published in June by George Mason University's Mercatus Center. Social Security is tied to the bond market because its trust funds are invested in special issue U.S. Treasury bonds. If Social Security reform is delayed, that may put upward pressure on Treasury yields, with investors wanting higher returns for long-term bonds. Delayed reform may either prompt higher interest rates and borrowing costs or inflationary adjustments that hurt the value of government liabilities, according to the Mercatus Center research. Those changes may affect household budgets through higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer credit, as well as student loans, according to the research. If interest rates and prices rise, that will interfere with economic growth, Akabas said."Those effects are also ones that the American people feel, in addition to adjustments to their benefits," Akabas said.Heading to the midterms, some Democratic congressional candidates have said they would raise or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap so high earners pay more into the program. In 2026, the 6.2% tax paid by both workers and their employers applies to earnings up to $184,500.Yet it remains to be seen whether Washington leaders will have the political will to address the problem soon. Tax increases, in particular, may not be viewed as politically popular heading into the 2028 presidential election.As such, payroll taxes are "extraordinarily unlikely" to rise in the next couple of years, said Jessica Riedl, a fellow at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center, which provides independent analyses of tax issues. If those tax hikes happen, it would likely be closer to 2032, she said."In Washington, they love to wait until the last minute," Riedl said. "There's no interest on either side for these sorts of tax increases in the short term. In the long term, I think everything is on the table."The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, founded by President Franklin Delano Roosevelt's son, former Congressman James Roosevelt, has scored incumbent lawmakers on whether their votes have protected those programs.The advocacy organization has also endorsed candidates that support raising payroll taxes and protecting Social Security benefits from cuts. With those endorsements, NCPSSM gives candidates a set of boxing gloves as a symbol of the fights they'll face in Congress, according to Dan Adcock, NCPSSM's director of government relations and policy.The organization is also working to educate voters that the senators elected this year will be among those to deal with Social Security, he said."We've been trying to impress upon voters why this is an issue that should be top tier," Adcock said. "They need to be asking candidates about what their plans for the program would be."

schema.headline: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries

title: Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed
description: watch nowDETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.Manufacturers
body: watch nowDETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs."At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jared Beck, head of Rivian's additive manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."The benefits of 3D printingAlso known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.The progression of the new steering wheel for Rivian's new R2 SUV from 3D print to finished design for production at its facility in Plymouth, Michigan.Michael Wayland / CNBCPrinters can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.Beck said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours."It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Beck said. The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.A 3D-printed version of Rivian's cartoon Yeti mascot named Gary stands inside an additive manufacturing area at Rivian's facility in Plymouth, Michigan.Michael Wayland / CNBC"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Beck said.Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.GM, FordThere's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer, holds up a device he 3D printed to reinstall vehicle badges onto the automaker's F-150 pickup trucks inside the River Rouge factory in Dearborn, Michigan. Michael Wayland / CNBC "By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost. Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.A table full of 3D-printed parts and tools inside the 3D-printing lab at Ford's River Rouge factory in Dearborn, Michigan.Michael Wayland / CNBC"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing. "The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."A GM metal model maker wipes dust from a 3D printer in between part builds at one of the Detroit automaker's facilities.Courtesy GM

schema.headline: Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed

title: Trump promised to slash energy costs  — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump promised voters angry about inflation that he would slash gas prices below $2 a gallon within his first year in office."My plan will cut energy prices in half or more than that within 12 months of taking office," Trump said in a speech to the New York Economic Club in September 2024 during his re-election campaign. "Energy was what caused our problem initially," he told voters. "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon."But when voters head to the ballot box on Tuesday energy prices will remain a headache. Gas and diesel prices are forecast to be the highest ever on an election day, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. "Prices have never been this high this late in the year," De Haan said. Gas prices stood at a national average of $4.20 a gallon on Friday, nearly 40% above the same period last year. The price of diesel, critical to transportation and agriculture, has surged about 70% over the past year, to $6.32 a gallon.During the 2022 U.S. midterm elections, the year that Russia invaded Ukraine and triggered an energy crisis, retail gas prices stood at $3.80, according to AAA data. Own goal"Trump got in his own way," De Haan said. "Back in December, we predicted that 2026 was going to be the cheapest year for gas since 2020. That required no effort. And obviously, it hasn't gone that way."Fuel prices have spiked since Trump decided to attack Iran in a joint attack with Israel on Feb. 28. Tehran retaliated with a wave of strikes on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, severely depressing oil flows through the vital shipping route.Trump told voters at a rally in Michigan last Sunday that rising fuel prices are a "small price to pay" to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. "Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement. The White House said gas prices when adjusted for inflation have been higher around previous election days.Exports through Hormuz have rebounded since the summer as the U.S. military helped ships through the strait. But the Middle East disruption has been compounded by Houthi rebel attacks on Saudi Arabian refineries, and Ukraine's strikes on refineries in Russia. Trump had promised to end that war in the first week of his second term, but the conflict is stuck in an intractable stalemate. "Frankly, diesel is the key crunch point here because it is so critical to economic growth," ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods told CNBC on Friday after the nation's largest oil company posted huge profits thanks to the disruptions.Airlines have hiked their fares to cover high costs from jet fuel, their biggest expense other than labor, hurting the fight to contain inflation. Political pressure Trump came under political pressure from Republicans to take action on fuel prices ahead of Tuesday's election. The cost of diesel is hurting big farm states like Iowa that have overwhelmingly backed Trump in his presidential campaigns. The senate race in the Hawkeye State has become competitive.Trump briefly contemplated a diesel export ban as Senator Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) lobbied to help the state's farmers. The president decided against it because it might also have raised gasoline prices. Instead, Trump issued an executive order to allow truckers to use tax-exempt, offroad diesel on U.S. highways, and announced an $8 billion relief program for farmers hit by high fuel prices. Trump later struck a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to export about 6 million barrels of diesel into the global market through November. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and even some Republican senators slammed the agreement as rewarding Russian aggression. Energy analysts said the diesel volumes in the Russia deal are small compared to global demand and won't have a meaningful impact on prices. More recently, crude oil prices have rallied ahead of the election. Trump has said he will not resume strikes on Iran before the midterms. But the market is pricing in the risk of another round of fighting after voting ends on Tuesday. International Brent crude oil prices are up more than 13% in October and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 15%."If there are escalations, that could obviously put upward pressure on prices just ahead of Thanksgiving," De Haan said, "which is also when Americans have really staunch traditions in terms of driving to friends and family."

schema.headline: Trump promised to slash energy costs  — but gasoline, diesel and jet fuel all soared instead

title: Halloween gets pricier as chocolate costs climb — Hershey may feel the pinch
description: Halloween candy is displayed at a Target store on Oct. 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesHalloween shopping got costli
body: Halloween candy is displayed at a Target store on Oct. 27, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesHalloween shopping got costlier this year as higher prices hit everything from the candy bowl to the pumpkin on your front porch. It's not only rough on consumers, but may also hit companies like Hershey.Americans are expected to spend $13.5 billion on Halloween, up from last year's record $13.1 billion, according to the National Retail Federation. "Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind," said Allison Zeller, NRF vice president of industry and consumer insights.Inflation is rippling through everything from candy to costumes. Pumpkins are costlier too. The average retail price reached $5.36 this year, up 11% from September 2020, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Drought reduced yields by roughly 30% to 40% in parts of Texas, a major pumpkin-growing state.Candy and chocolateCandy remains one of the biggest expenses this Halloween and prices increases are running ahead of broader food inflation, though the rate of increase has slowed. Candy and chewing gum prices were up 7.7% in September from a year earlier, according to the latest Consumer Price Index data. The sugar-and-sweets category increased 5.5% over the same period. Adverse weather, including the impact of El Niño, tightened the outlook for sugar supply. Unusually wet conditions disrupted Brazil's sugarcane harvest, while drought and other weather extremes affected production in other major growing regions."As Halloween swiftly approaches, candy stands out in the grocery store as one of the more expensive categories, relative to prices last year," food economist Richard Volpe wrote on LinkedIn. "In past years, this has left me swimming with candy," he added. "As I write this, Halloween is days away and I have a paltry three bags of candy sitting on my desk."Nielsen IQ Early Market data showed Halloween candy sales down 11.7% through September 19. Four weeks later, the decline narrowed to 6.7%, with chocolate at -7.2% and confection at -5.3%, according to the report.Chocolate so far has been the most vulnerable, especially after a disruption in cocoa supply in West Africa, which was hit by poor growing conditions in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana. A potential El Niño and dry Harmattan trade winds could put pressure on the 2026-27 West African cocoa crop.There was some relief in commodity markets after cocoa prices fell sharply from its historic highs, according to David Branch, sector manager at the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.But that drop has yet to translate into cheaper chocolates.Wells Fargo Agri-Food estimates chocolate prices will be about 8% higher than last Halloween, with effective transaction prices rising roughly 5% to 8% after promotions. Much of the chocolate on shelves this Halloween was produced using cocoa bought six to 12 months earlier."The worst of the cocoa crisis has passed, but price relief hasn't reached store shelves yet," Branch told CNBC. "For chocolate manufacturers, the principal 2026 issue is no longer simply cocoa availability. It is the timing mismatch between falling futures, high-cost inventories, retailer negotiations, and consumer elasticity."Halloween chocolate dollar sales were down 7.2% from a year earlier through the nine weeks ended Oct. 17, according to NIQ, with weakness in milk chocolate leading the decline. NIQ estimates Halloween chocolate sales to be down $33.1 million from last year, with milk chocolate accounting for a $34.4 million decline. Dark chocolate, meanwhile, gained $2.3 million. Overall Halloween candy, gum and mint sales were down 6.7%. To help juice sales, retailers are offering discounts — Walmart and Target have flash deals and heavy discounts on items from candy to Halloween costumes. Candy shoppers, meanwhile, appear to be moving toward smaller packages. Small candy packs of nine ounces or less are up 24% in dollar terms and 14% in units, while every larger package size is declining, according to NIQ. Wells Fargo expects shoppers to increasingly favor value packs and alternatives that use less cocoa, including gummies, sour candy, wafers and caramel."Consumers will continue buying candy, but shopping baskets are likely to contain fewer chocolate pieces, more value packs, and a greater share of gummies, sour products, wafers, caramel, and other lower-cocoa alternatives," Branch said.Hershey stock was rising on Friday as consumers ditched AI stocks for safer consumer staples. But analysts see trouble brewing for the candy maker. The company, which reported third quarter results on Thursday, lowered its 2026 organic sales growth forecast to 3% (from 3%-3.5%). That implies "flattish" organic growth in the fourth quarter, according to Jefferies analyst Scott MarksHershey's commentary was "incrementally cautious," he added in a note, saying "consumer and cost pressures" are weighing on the near-term outlook.    "We're looking at areas like in convenience as you see a consumer that's under pressure to give more value and drive pricing through bespoke promotions versus overall price decreases," Hershey CEO Kirk Tanner told analysts on an earnings call.Marks cut his price target on the stock to $170, joining cuts at brokerages such as DA Davidson, BNP Paribas, Bernstein and Deutsche Bank. Consensus estimates for 2027 earnings fell 3.7% to $9.49 a share, according to FactSet.CNBC's Alex Harring contributed to the reporting.

schema.headline: Halloween gets pricier as chocolate costs climb — Hershey may feel the pinch

title: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns
description: CEO of Meta Platforms Mark Zuckerberg attends a press briefing held by U.S. President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificia
body: CEO of Meta Platforms Mark Zuckerberg attends a press briefing held by U.S. President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesMeta's outlook has been revised downward by S&P Global Ratings on concerns surrounding cash flow and AI spending.The credit agency said Friday that the outlook reflects "uncertainty" about Meta's elevated capex and its negative free cash flow. Meta's credit rating was revised from AA- stable to AA- negative, S&P said. S&Ps highest credit rating is AAA. Anything below BBB falls into the junk bond category. The agency questioned "Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments" relative to its peers, which are also spending heavily on data center buildouts and going cash flow negative in the process. Although Meta has recently debuted its Muse AI agent app and related foundation models, S&P said "it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years."A Meta spokesperson pushed back on the revision."We respectfully disagree with S&P's assertion about Meta's AI monetization capabilities," the spokesperson said in a statement. "We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile." Meta said in its third-quarter earnings report last week that it expects full-year capex to come in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also posted negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, going in the red for the first time.Investors sent Meta shares down 7% following the report despite a revenue beat. The stock finished October down 15%, its worst month in four years. The company said on Monday that it plans to raise $95 billion to help fund its AI initiatives, with plans to first raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, followed by an additional $60 billion through an at-the-market program.S&P said that while it expects Meta's capex growth to start "flattening out beginning in 2028," the agency is "less certain that it will curtail its spending as previously anticipated."WATCH: Mike Khouw likes this options strategy for Meta post-earnings.watch now

schema.headline: Meta outlook revised downward by S&P on cash flow and capex concerns

title: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered
description: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesBinance said Sunday that it has resumed withdrawals of bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies following the record theft
body: Visual China Group | Getty ImagesBinance said Sunday that it has resumed withdrawals of bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies following the record theft of around $6.3 billion in token assets from its hot wallets."First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals is $BTC bitcoin network," Binance said in an X post.It later said withdrawals have also been restored for the Ethereum Network and BNB Smart Chain.The exchange said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the assets in the heist announced Thursday.Separately, the FBI said late Saturday that ​it has determined North ​Korea ​was responsible for the ⁠theft. Binance also said it will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and over-the-counter channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens."All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users."The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets."Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said.Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said.Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement.It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place. The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.North Korea responsible for theftThe FBI said malicious North Korean actors laundered Binance's stolen ‌assets by ‌converting them into Ethereum. The agency expects that the thieves will convert the digital assets as they prepare them for "further laundering stages."TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, had initially pointed to North Korean hackers as the culprits."Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said.— CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano, Davis Giangiulio, Terri Cullen and Azhar Sukri contributed to this report.watch now

schema.headline: Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered

title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety
description: A bitcoin automated teller machine (ATM) stands at the Coin Trader bitcoin retail store in Tokyo, Japan, on Wednesday, Aug. 30, 2017. Stock of Bitcoin
body: A bitcoin automated teller machine (ATM) stands at the Coin Trader bitcoin retail store in Tokyo, Japan, on Wednesday, Aug. 30, 2017. Stock of Bitcoin, the best-known digital currency, has surged 358 percent this year. While staggering, lesser-known competitors have seen even bigger gains, such as the more than 4,000 percent increase for ethereum. Photographer: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesTwo high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange.A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents. Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. Questions over the safety of users' funds"I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place."For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan, CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this."Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. Vulnerabilities on offshore platformsA key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoinbase v. Robinhood 1-day. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today."Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X. "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach, though the company didn't specify what they were. A unique target in a changing landscapeFalk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach.It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added.

title: Trump defamation suit against Murdoch, WSJ over Epstein letter dismissed with prejudice
description: U.S. President Donald Trump and Rupert Murdoch. Kevin Lamarque | Ricky Carioti | Via ReutersA federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejud
body: U.S. President Donald Trump and Rupert Murdoch. Kevin Lamarque | Ricky Carioti | Via ReutersA federal judge in Miami on Saturday dismissed with prejudice President Donald Trump's amended defamation lawsuit against media baron Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal over the newspaper's reporting on a purported 50th birthday letter from the president to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.District Court Judge Darrin Gayles ruled that Trump had again failed to plausibly allege the newspaper and other defendants acted with actual malice when they published the story in July 2025."As with his first attempt, he has failed," Gayles wrote in the 20-page ruling, which came more than six months after he dismissed Trump's first version of the suit. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation."By dismissing the suit with prejudice, the judge blocked Trump from filing another suit alleging the same claims about Murdoch and the paper in federal court.Gayles said the Journal had conducted a "thoughtful and detailed investigation," and he rejected Trump's argument that the newspaper should not have published the story after he denied writing the letter.The judge did not determine whether Trump actually authored the disputed letter. Trump has adamantly denied writing it.When Galyes first dismissed the suit in April, he allowed Trump to file an amended version of the complaint to cure legal defects the judge had identified.  Trump was seeking $10 billion in damages from Murdoch and the Journal, which is owned by Murdoch's News Corp. A spokesperson for the newspaper's publisher, Dow Jones & Co., in a statement to CNBC on Saturday, said, "We're pleased with the court's decision."A spokesman for Trump's legal team confirmed to CNBC that the president plans to appeal the ruling."President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants," the spokesman said in a statement. "The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions."Gayles, as he did when dismissing the suit for the first time, noted Trump, who has adamantly denied sending the letter to his then-friend Epstein in 2003, had "not plausibly alleged that the Defendants published the Article with actual malice."Plaintiffs who are public figures like Trump must show a defendant acted with actual malice when making allegedly defamatory statements, according to Supreme Court decisions that Gayles cited at the beginning of his ruling.Trump's amended lawsuit contained new details and claims, including that Murdoch told the president "I will handle it" during a phone conversation they had about an article describing a birthday letter to Epstein that allegedly bore Trump's signature, Newsweek previously reported.Gayles rejected each of Trump's arguments in the amended complaint, including that the Journal did not adequately investigate the letter, omitted relevant details, and that the article was published after the president and his representatives denied it was authentic.Gayles said that accepting that last argument would effectively allow public figures to block unfavorable reporting, which "runs afoul of the First Amendment" that protects freedom of speech and the press.Saturday's ruling is the latest setback in litigation between Trump and the media.Another federal judge in Miami on Oct. 22 ordered Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.A birthday letter that U.S. President Donald Trump allegedly wrote to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein more than 20 years ago is seen as presented by the Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives on their X account September 8, 2025.Democrats on the House Oversight CommitteeThe Journal's article on July 17, 2025, said a letter bearing Trump's signature was included in an album of letters Epstein was giving for his 50th birthday. The article said Trump sent the letter at the request of Epstein's close friend, Ghislaine Maxwell, who two decades later was convicted of procuring underage girls to be sexually abused by Epstein.The Journal noted that the letter "contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker.""A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly 'Donald' below her waist, mimicking pubic hair," Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo said in the article."The letter concludes: 'Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,'" they wrote.Trump angrily denied writing the letter, saying, "This is not me. This is a fake thing."'"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," the president said at the time.

title: The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know
description: Voters fill out their ballots at an early voting polling place at Lynnhurst Recreation Center on Oct. 28, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Stephen Matur
body: Voters fill out their ballots at an early voting polling place at Lynnhurst Recreation Center on Oct. 28, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota.Stephen Maturen | Getty ImagesThe outcome of Tuesday's election is expected to have broad implications across the market, including municipal bonds. The spotlight has been on the battle for congressional control and whether Democrats will wrest the House of Representatives, the Senate or both from Republicans. But for the muni market, what happens at the state level could have bigger repercussions — at least in the near term. There is an array of initiatives on ballots around the nation that could change tax laws and add to bond supply. Taxes matter to muni investors since the income received is free of federal tax, as well as state tax if the holder lives in the state where the bond is issued.Red vs. blue taxes Depending on the location, ballot measures are up for approval that would either provide tax breaks, or raise taxes on the wealthy. "It's a complete bifurcation between red and blue states," said Dan Close, head of municipals at Nuveen. "Blue states are trying to put in place graduated income tax structures, trying to capture more revenue from high-income earners. Red states are promoting affordability by trying to cut property taxes."Red states are those that predominantly vote Republican, while blue states swing toward Democrats. For instance, California has a proposition known as the "billionaire tax," which would impose a one-time levy equal to 5% of the wealth of certain taxpayers with at least $1 billion in assets. The state also has a measure on the ballot that would make a temporary tax hike permanent on individuals earning over $371,000, adjusted annually for inflation. The tax is currently set to expire in 2031. "The impact to the muni bond market will be to make the exemption more valuable," Close said of the possible passage of tax increases. Investors will likely seek shelter in the muni market, which would send bond prices higher, he noted.It is a different story in Florida, where voters are set to decide whether to increase the Sunshine State's homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes. Qualified homeowners currently have a $25,000 property tax exemption, as well as another for $25,000 that doesn't apply to school property taxes. The new proposal raises the latter exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 by 2028. New residents have a five-year waiting period before receiving the benefit.  If passed, some local governments will have to find other revenue sources or increase the overall tax rate to replace what they've lost, said Tom Kozlik, head of public policy and municipal strategy at HilltopSecurities."It's not necessarily going to result in downgrades for sure, but there would have to be some balancing with regard to overall revenues," he said.Not all municipalities will be hurt equally, which means credit research is important, said Close."Like everything in municipal finance, it is really on a case-by-case basis that you could have some credit deterioration from [a] rollback of property taxes," he said. Increased supplyOther voters on Tuesday will be asked to approve more state or local government debt. That could weigh on a market that has already seen heightened supply. Some $473.8 billion has already been issued year to date, through September, according to the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association. That's a 7.8% increase over the same period a year ago. In 2025, total muni issuance reached $587.3 billion, 14.3% higher than 2024, Sifma said. Cooper Howard, director of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, believes supply is the biggest issue coming out of the election. "That amount of issuance has been one of the reasons why you have to see that strong amount of demand continue to keep pace with it for total returns to keep up," Howard said. Fortunately, new supply doesn't necessarily come quickly into the market. "There's a window over a couple years that they can issue," he noted. The ultimate makeup of the next Congress could also have consequences for muni investors as lawmakers sort out their priorities. Most notable is what lawmakers will do to tackle the country's affordability problem, Kozlik at Hilltop said. "There could be some tax policy initiatives and even affordability-related initiatives that manifest themselves in the first quarter of next year," he said. "That could impact housing. It could impact higher education. It could impact public power financing."Opportunities now Investors considering moves before the election may want to look at those states with tax increases on the ballot, said Close at Nuveen.For instance, Nuveen recently began offering a separately managed account dedicated to Washington after getting an enormous number of inquiries from financial advisors. The state recently enacted a 9.9% tax on individuals with taxable annual income above $1 million, set to go into effect in 2028. But the issue is now being put to voters, who can decide whether to repeal the new law.  "At the margin, if you do think that some of these measures are going to pass, knowing that bonds usually move up with an increase in taxes, there might be some opportunities to buy ahead of the election for blue states," Close said.Howard believes munis are attractive right now, particularly for those who are in a tax bracket of 24% or above. Fundamentals are good and the bonds largely have good credit quality, he said. "About 70% of the broad muni index is either triple-A or double-A rated."Kozlik is also bullish, calling yields "really attractive." He suggests investors concentrate on AA-rated or higher bonds. "The muni space is part of the portfolio that most investors want," he said. "It helps them sleep well at night."

schema.headline: The midterm election could reshape the muni bond market. Here’s what investors need to know

title: Trump called out Big Oil profits. Here’s how much their refining earnings have surged since
description: Chevron does not report a comparable, standalone refining-margin figure, but it reported Friday that its downstream earnings more than quadrupled from
body: Chevron does not report a comparable, standalone refining-margin figure, but it reported Friday that its downstream earnings more than quadrupled from a year earlier to $4.9 billion, with the company citing higher margins on refined-product sales.That's amid tight supplies of refined fuels and pressure on refinery output globally, despite oil firms reporting this week that they are running their facilities near capacity to try to meet demand.Why supply is tightAlong with soaring refined product margins, higher crude oil prices have also supported earnings at some integrated oil majors, which operate both upstream oil-and-gas businesses and downstream refining operations.Their profits have climbed back toward levels last seen during the energy shock of 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The earnings spikes are in sharp contrast to consumers facing higher energy prices.watch nowSome analysts say political efforts to tackle prices — release of emergency diesel stockpiles and a U.S. deal with Russia to supply more diesel to the global market — may have only a limited impact unless they materially increase available supply, demand weakens or global tensions ease.Raphael Portela, director for corporate strategy and analytics at energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie, told CNBC that crude oil barrels were still "getting out of the Gulf" amid the war, but "at a steep freight premium," while "the diesel and jet fuel those barrels would have become largely aren't.""Russia's refinery outages and export ban have taken a second slug out of the global pool," he added.He listed what would have to happen for the crunch to end: "Product supply coming back, based on greater crude availability to the global refining sector: Gulf refineries restarting and Russian exports returning."A Hormuz settlement would hit margins quickly on sentiment, but with inventories this depleted, the physical tightness carries well into 2027."Read more

title: Companies promised AI gains — here's how the payoff showed up in earnings
description: The dollar steadied on Wednesday after the United States launched strikes against Iran, while investors awaited key U.S. inflation data.Skaman306 | Mo
body: The dollar steadied on Wednesday after the United States launched strikes against Iran, while investors awaited key U.S. inflation data.Skaman306 | Moment | Getty ImagesSome companies are beginning to report financial benefits from artificial intelligence investments, as interest in the technology shifts from hype to measurable returns in the latest quarter.Corporate AI investment has surged as companies look to boost efficiency and become more profitable, reaching $581.7 billion in 2025, up 130% from the previous year, according to the Stanford HAI 2026 AI Index report.As CEOs tout the tech's benefits and hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta are expected to spend $700 billion combined this year on its infrastructure, investors are looking for measurable gains. Now, with third-quarter earnings season underway, some companies are beginning to put numbers around those benefits.Santander puts a number on AI gainsSpanish banking giant Santander said Wednesday that it saw AI initiatives generate 194 million euros ($216 million) in business value in the first nine months of 2026. Santander Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera told CNBC that AI is helping the bank reduce low-value tasks so employees can focus on higher-value work. "This affects both revenue and costs, so we are actually in the quarter where we can actually link directly to AI a positive contribution," Cantera said."AI is being embedded in all the processes that we are conducting at the bank, so it's really difficult to just say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients."Novartis and Standard Chartered see AI in resultsSwiss pharmaceutical giant Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC that AI was beginning to contribute to the company's bottom line.Novartis reported third-quarter core operating income of $6.04 billion, up 10% year on year at constant currencies. The company did not quantify how much of that was attributable to AI but Narasimhan told CNBC: "I think this is the first quarter I've really seen AI start to improve actually our P&L on a tangible basis.""We're working on R&D [research & development] to see if it can really increase R&D productivity," Narasimhan said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.watch now"We're already seeing some of the productivity you saw in the bottom-line performance of what we can do with AI from M&S [marketing & sales]."Meanwhile, Standard Chartered Chief Financial Officer Manus Costello told "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the company is seeing AI "appear everywhere across the business."The bank reported third-quarter operating income growth of 14% at constant currency, excluding notable items."I think you can see it in the top line growth that we're delivering, and you can see it in that operating leverage that I talked about," Costello said, adding that AI is helping managers build better customer relationships and generate more income. watch now"We're also seeing that strong operating leverage that I talked about, where income is growing much faster than costs, and some of that is because we've been able to deploy AI tools to improve core processes and enable us to scale those up very efficiently," he added.Carlsberg says benefits are not yet at scaleCarlsberg CEO Jacob Aarup-Andersen said on "Squawk Box Europe" this week that it's not seeing AI benefits at scale, but the technology has impacted internal processes, cost efficiency, commercial and pricing processes, marketing and its supply chain. The company's revenue grew 4.9% in the third quarter.Big Tech points to AI-driven growthElsewhere, tech firms are also reporting gains. Meta said in its Oct. 21 earnings that its AI investments were delivering "substantial incremental advertising revenue," while total revenue jumped 26% in the quarter ended Sept. 30.While Alphabet's Google Search revenue growth slowed amid concerns about AI competition, Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to nearly $31 billion in the third quarter, it reported on Wednesday.

schema.headline: Companies promised AI gains — here's how the payoff showed up in earnings

title: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months
description: Jetcityimage | Istock | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds. Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5
body: Jetcityimage | Istock | Getty ImagesThe U.S. Department of the Treasury has announced new rates for Series I bonds. Newly purchased I bonds will pay 5.51% annual interest from Nov. 1 through April 30, which is up from the 4.26% yield offered on purchases made through Oct. 31.The new rate includes a variable portion of 4.08% based on inflation data, and a fixed portion of 1.40%. The fixed rate is up from 0.90% announced in April, and the highest since 2006. Combined, the composite I bond rate is 5.51% after rounding, according to the Treasury. Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026Amid the post-pandemic inflation peak, the I bond rate hit a record high of 9.62% in May 2022, and investors poured millions into the government-backed, nearly risk-free asset. As inflation cooled and I bond rates fell, many short-term investors redeemed I bonds. But investors could return as inflation pushes I bond rates back up, experts say. "I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point," said David Enna, founder of Tipswatch.com, a website that tracks Treasury inflation-protected securities, or TIPS, and I bond rates.  I bonds are a lot more attractive at this point.David EnnaFounder of Tipswatch.comThe consumer price index rose 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from an annual pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.In September, some higher inflation came from the Iran war, which pushed up gasoline and energy costs. President Donald Trump's tariffs, new artificial intelligence data centers and demand for travel have also added to rising prices, economists say. Consumers expect rising inflation to continue. In September, the one-year inflation outlook jumped to 3.9%, the highest in more than three years, according to a New York Fed survey released in early October. How I bond rates workI bond rates have a variable and fixed rate portion, which the Treasury adjusts every six months, in May and November. The variable rate is tied to inflation — using the consumer price index percentage change over six months — and stays the same for six months after you purchase, regardless of the Treasury's next update. Your fixed rate doesn't change after purchasing I bonds. The Treasury doesn't disclose how it calculates fixed-rate adjustments, making it harder to predict.Some experts believe the I bond fixed rate could be driven by real, or inflation-adjusted, yields from five-year TIPS, according to Ken Tumin, founder of DepositQuest.com, a blog that tracks I bond rates, among other deposit accounts. "There's some uncertainty there," Tumin said.   How the change affects current I bond investorsIf you currently own I bonds, rate updates follow a six-month timeline based on your original purchase date. After you own I bonds for six months, the variable yield changes to the next announced rate. But the fixed rate stays the same for the entire time you own the asset.For example, let's say you purchased I bonds in March when the variable rate was still 3.12% and the fixed rate was 0.9%. After six months, the variable portion would shift to 3.34%, announced in April 2026, but your fixed rate would remain 0.9%.You can earn I bond interest for up to 30 years, or less if you redeem the assets before that. However, you can't cash in I bonds for at least one year after you buy them. If you redeem within five years, you lose your last three months of interest.

schema.headline: Treasury Department announces new Series I bond rate of 5.51% for the next six months

title: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans
description: Abraham Gonzalez Fernandez | E+ | Getty ImagesLeaving a job can make a small 401(k) hard to hold on to: Some employers' plans cash out accounts under
body: Abraham Gonzalez Fernandez | E+ | Getty ImagesLeaving a job can make a small 401(k) hard to hold on to: Some employers' plans cash out accounts under $1,000 or move slightly larger balances into an IRA. Taking the money in cash and moving on can feel like the simplest option, but it can have short- and long-term financial consequences.A system backed by major 401(k) administrators aims to make it easier for those savings to follow workers to their next job. New research from one of those companies, Vanguard, shows it's helping fewer people cash out — although most of the money has yet to reach workers' new retirement plans.Among workers with less than $1,000 in their 401(k), the share who cashed out within 10 months of leaving their job fell to about 9% from roughly 50% after their employers began participating in a new system called the Portability Services Network, according to the Vanguard research. Among those with balances of between $1,000 and $7,000, the share cashing out fell to 31% from 39%.Portability Services Network is a coalition of large 401(k) administrators — including Vanguard, Fidelity Investments and Alight Solutions, among others — in conjunction with Retirement Clearinghouse and has been in operation since late 2023.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyMidterm elections: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisionsCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026How it works: When a worker with a small 401(k) balance leaves an employer that participates in the network, the money is generally automatically rolled into a safe harbor IRA, where it remains until the network matches it with the worker's new employer plan. The balance then gets rolled into the new 401(k) from that interim IRA. The catch, however, is that the receiving employer must also participate in the network for the money to move to the next employer's plan.In Vanguard's research, just 6% of accounts that have been transferred into IRAs as part of this automatic portability network successfully made it to a new employer's plan as of early 2026, largely because few employers have opted in. The rest generally remained in those interim IRAs, waiting to be matched with another employer plan that participates in the network. While workers can always roll over the money into their new 401(k) themselves, the point of the network is for it to happen automatically.Of the roughly 220,000 outbound rollovers involving Vanguard participants analyzed, the median balance was just $200, and nearly three-quarters involved less than $1,000. The typical saver affected was 31 years old, earned about $20,000 annually and had worked for their employer for roughly six months, according to the research.The cash-out analysis is based on workers at 83 employer-sponsored retirement plans administered by Vanguard that have adopted the automatic portability.Financial consequences of cashing outTypically, when you part ways with an employer, you can leave your money in its 401(k) plan if the account value is above $7,000. Balances under $1,000 usually result in the plan cashing you out and mailing you a check. For amounts between $1,000 and $7,000, most plans roll the balance over to an IRA if the former employee takes no action to move it themselves.Cashing out a 401(k) when leaving a job, whether done by an employer or the employee, can have lasting financial consequences. Workers who withdraw their savings can owe income taxes on the money and may face a 10% early withdrawal penalty if they're younger than 59½. They also lose the opportunity for that money to grow over time.watch nowMost workers — 84% — have changed employers at least once during their careers, while 53% have switched three or more times and 27% have made at least five moves, according to a new study from Empower, a 401(k) recordkeeper and a founding partner of the portability network. The report is based on an online survey of 2,005 adults.Additionally, 50% of Generation Z respondents and 45% of millennials said they may have retirement savings from a previous employer that they've lost track of, the survey found. That compares with 30% of Gen X and 14% of baby boomers.$71.3 million in assets have made it to new plansSince the Portability Services Network's launch in November 2023, there have been 53,118 completed transactions, totaling $71.3 million in assets transferred from a previous employer plan to a new employer plan via automatic portability, according to Steve Holman, senior vice president of Portability Services Network strategy and development at Retirement Clearinghouse.There are 23,787 plans that have adopted automatic portability, representing 7.73 million participants, Holman said. The overall estimate of participants in 401(k)s and similar workplace plans is about 96 million, he said.watch nowThere are 1.22 million eligible participants waiting to be matched with a new employer, up more than 25% since the beginning of 2026, Holman said.Snags remain with the automatic portability processKeeping the money in a safe harbor IRA can be better for investors financially than cashing out — but management fees may take a toll on small balances, especially when the money is in an interest-bearing cash account or other conservative investment."For many of these small accounts, earnings on the conservative default investment may not be sufficient to offset recurring account-level fees while the account remains unmatched, leaving the balance vulnerable to gradual erosion," the Vanguard study said.Workers with Roth savings face another complication. If retirement savings are in a traditional 401(k) — funded with pretax contributions and taxed when withdrawn in retirement — it goes into a traditional IRA. Likewise, Roth 401(k)s, funded with after-tax contributions and withdrawn tax-free down the road, go into Roth IRAs. However, IRS rules don't allow for a Roth IRA to be rolled into a new employer's 401(k), even a Roth 401(k)."We are advocating for future legislation to allow for Roth dollars to be eligible for auto-portability — our technology can support it today," Holman said.

schema.headline: Automatic 401(k) rollovers reduce cash-outs, research finds — but few accounts reach new employer plans
